scope.start: 11a: the Gemara returns to the Mishnah and asks for Beit Shammai's reason for a dinar (R. Zeira)
scope.end: 11b: R. Shimon ben Lakish's derivation from the Hebrew maidservant and the objection to it (resolved on 12a)

sections.title: Beit Shammai's Dinar: Dignity, Tyrian Coinage or the Hebrew Maidservant?
sections.gist: Three explanations for Beit Shammai's minimum of a dinar: a woman's dignity (R. Zeira), Rav Asi's rule on Tyrian coinage (Rav Yosef), and the Hebrew maidservant's deduction from her price (R. Shimon ben Lakish).

bullets.text: The Mishnah: for betrothal by money, Beit Shammai require at least a dinar, while Beit Hillel allow a *perutah* or a *perutah*'s worth. The Gemara asks for Beit Shammai's reasoning.
If the money of betrothal is a formal act of transfer, why should the amount matter at all? And why a dinar in particular?
The gap is large. A dinar is about 192 *perutot*, and a *sela* is four dinars, or 768 *perutot*.

chart.caption: Three explanations of Beit Shammai's minimum of a dinar
columns: How it fares on this daf
rows: R. Zeira

A presumption about her wishes
Abaye's objection from R. Yannai's daughters limits it to betrothal at night or through an agent
Rav Yosef (Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav Asi)
Torah money is Tyrian, and the smallest Tyrian silver coin is a dinar

The rule is later restricted to set sums, and betrothal money has no set sum
R. Shimon ben Lakish (following Chizkiya)
Betrothal follows the Hebrew maidservant, whose price must allow deduction
*Ve'hefdah* (Shemot 21:8)
Objection: perhaps a *perutah* sale simply allows no deduction

children.title: *Isha Makpedet al Atzmah*: A Woman's Dignity, and R. Yannai's Daughters
children.gist: R. Zeira grounds the dinar in a woman's dignity. Abaye's objection from R. Yannai's daughters narrows the rule to cases where she can't see what she receives.

bullets.text: R. Zeira: a woman is particular about herself (*isha makpedet al atzmah*) and won't agree to be betrothed for less than a dinar.
Abaye objects. R. Yannai's daughters wouldn't agree to less than three *kav* of dinars. If one of them reaches out her hand and accepts one dinar from a man, would you say she isn't betrothed?

R. Zeira: my rule doesn't cover a woman who reaches out and accepts, since she may waive her own dignity. It covers a betrothal at night, when she can't see what she is given, or through an agent she sent without naming a sum. There we presume she would accept no less than a dinar.
The weakness of this reason is that dignity is subjective. It varies from woman to woman, and the rule must be qualified the moment she acts against it.

So Beit Shammai's dinar becomes a presumption about women's wishes, while Beit Hillel's *perutah* is an objective floor: the smallest sum the law treats as money. That invites a more principled explanation.

illustration.caption: R. Zeira's reason for Beit Shammai at work: at night or through an agent she is presumed to want at least a dinar, but a woman who knowingly takes less than her standard, like R. Yannai's daughter taking one dinar, is betrothed (11a).

children.title: Rav Yosef: Rav Asi's Rule of *Kesef Tzuri* and *Kesef Medinah*
children.gist: Rav Yosef explains Beit Shammai by Rav Asi's rule on Tyrian and provincial coinage. The Gemara tests the rule against four Torah cases, restricts it to set sums, and asks what it adds.

children.title: Torah Money Is Tyrian, So the Minimum Is a Silver Dinar
children.gist: Rav Yosef: Beit Shammai follow Rav Asi's rule that the Torah's money is Tyrian coinage, whose smallest silver coin is the dinar.

bullets.text: Rav Yosef: Beit Shammai follow Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav Asi. Every sum of money in the Torah is *kesef Tzuri*, Tyrian coinage, and every sum set by the Sages is *kesef medinah*, provincial coinage.
Provincial coinage was worth about an eighth of Tyrian. Beit Shammai take the Torah's standard, and the smallest Tyrian silver coin is the dinar.
The two systems use the same coin names. A sum stated as a *sela* or a dinar therefore means eight times as much in one system as in the other.

children.title: Is Every "Money" in the Torah Tyrian? Four Challenges
children.gist: The Gemara tests Rav Asi's rule against admission to part of a claim, *ma'aser sheni*, *hekdesh* and betrothal. The first three have answers; betrothal does not.

bullets.text: The Gemara takes up the rule itself: is it really established that every "money" in the Torah means at least a silver dinar?

chart.caption: Four places where the Torah says "money" and less than a Tyrian dinar suffices
rows: Admission to part of a claim
"Money or vessels to guard" (Shemot 22:6)
A claim of two silver *ma'ah*; an admission of a *perutah*
"Money" is read with "vessels": at least two, and significant
*Ma'aser sheni*
"And bind up the money in your hand" (Devarim 14:25)
Copper coins (Mishnah Ma'aser Sheni 2:8)
"The money": the article includes any coin
*Hekdesh*
"And he will give the money" (Vayikra 27)
Something worth a *perutah* (Shmuel)
*Gezeirah shavah* "money" from *ma'aser sheni*
Betrothal
"When a man takes a woman" (Devarim 24:1), with "taking" from Ephron's field
A *perutah* (Beit Hillel)
None: is Rav Asi following only Beit Shammai? The rule is restated

children.title: *Modeh Be'miktzat*: Why a Claim of Two Silver *Ma'ah* Suffices
children.gist: The oath of one who admits part of a claim needs a claim of only two silver *ma'ah*, though the Torah says "money"; the answer is that "money" is read together with "vessels".

bullets.text: The Torah's case of a deposit says "If a man deliver to his neighbor money or vessels to guard" (Shemot 22:6). Yet the Mishnah in Shevuot requires, for the judges' oath of one who admits part of a claim, a claim of only two silver *ma'ah* and an admission of a *perutah*. How, if Torah money is Tyrian?
Answer: "money" is juxtaposed with "vessels". Just as "vessels" means at least two, "money" means at least two coins, and just as money is significant, the vessels must be significant too.

children.title: *Ma'aser Sheni*: "*Ha'kesef*", "The Money", Includes Copper
children.gist: *Ma'aser sheni* may be redeemed with copper coins, which the Gemara explains from the article in "the money".

bullets.text: The Torah says of *ma'aser sheni*: "And bind up the money in your hand" (Devarim 14:25). Yet the Mishnah (Ma'aser Sheni 2:8) discusses exchanging copper coins of *ma'aser sheni* for a *sela*, so copper serves as its money.
Answer: the verse says *ha'kesef*, "the money". The article is an amplification and includes any coin.

children.title: *Hekdesh*: Redeemed for a *Perutah*'s Worth, Learned from *Ma'aser Sheni*
children.gist: Shmuel lets *hekdesh* be redeemed for a *perutah*'s worth; the Gemara traces this to a *gezeirah shavah* from *ma'aser sheni*.

bullets.text: The Torah says of redeeming *hekdesh*: "And he will give the money and it will be assured to him." Yet Shmuel: *hekdesh* worth a hundred dinars that was redeemed with something worth a *perutah* is redeemed.
Answer: Shmuel learns "money" here from "money" of *ma'aser sheni* by *gezeirah shavah*, so here too any coin works.

children.title: Betrothal: Does Rav Asi Follow Only Beit Shammai?
children.gist: Betrothal money is learned from the Torah, yet Beit Hillel allow a *perutah*; this challenge has no answer.

bullets.text: Betrothal is learned from "When a man takes a woman" (Devarim 24:1), with "taking" compared by *gezeirah shavah* to "taking" at the field of Ephron. Yet Beit Hillel allow a *perutah*.
Shall we say, then, that Rav Asi stated his rule only according to Beit Shammai? The Gemara gives no direct answer and restates the rule instead.

children.title: Restated: Only *Kesef Katzuv*, a Set Sum in the Torah, Is Tyrian
children.gist: Rav Asi's rule is recast. Only a set sum in the Torah is Tyrian and the Sages' set sums are provincial, while "money" with no sum can be any coin.

bullets.text: "Rather, if it was stated, it was stated like this": every set sum of money in the Torah is Tyrian, and every sum set by the Sages is provincial.

The line now runs between a fixed number (*kesef katzuv*) and money mentioned with no sum. Where the Torah gives a number, it means the heavy Tyrian coin; where it just says "money", a *perutah* will do.
This answers the challenges, but it also takes away Rav Yosef's basis for Beit Shammai: the Torah sets no sum for betrothal money, so another source for the dinar is needed.

children.title: What Rav Asi Adds: The Sages' *Sela* Is Half a Dinar
children.gist: The Torah's set sums in sacred shekels are already in the Mishnah in Bekhorot. Rav Asi's point is that a rabbinic fine, like the *sela* for striking another, is a provincial *sela* of half a dinar.

bullets.text: What does Rav Asi teach? The Mishnah (Bekhorot 49b) already lists the Torah's set sums: five *sela* to redeem a firstborn son, thirty for a slave killed by an ox, fifty from a rapist or a seducer, a hundred from a defamer. All are paid in the sacred shekel, in Tyrian coinage.

His point is the second half, which that Mishnah doesn't teach. A *baraita*: one who strikes another in disrespect gives him a *sela*. It is not a Tyrian *sela* of four dinars but a provincial *sela* of half a dinar, which people call an *istira*.
Half a dinar against four dinars is exactly the one-to-eight ratio: the provincial *sela* is the *istira*.

The weightiest application is the *ketubah*. A virgin's *ketubah* is two hundred *zuz*. Those who hold that the *ketubah* is rabbinic read these as provincial *zuz*, worth twenty-five Tyrian *zuz*, so the question whether it is biblical or rabbinic changes the sum eightfold.

children.title: R. Shimon ben Lakish: The Hebrew Maidservant's Price Must Allow Deduction
children.gist: R. Shimon ben Lakish grounds Beit Shammai in Chizkiya's reading of *ve'hefdah*: a Hebrew maidservant deducts from her price, and a *perutah* can't be reduced. The Gemara objects that a *perutah* sale might simply allow no deduction.

bullets.text: R. Shimon ben Lakish: Beit Shammai follow Chizkiya, who reads "Then he shall let her be redeemed" (*ve'hefdah*, Shemot 21:8) as a deduction (*gira'on*). A Hebrew maidservant (*amah ivriyah*) who comes into money may go free early, paying her price less the work she has done.
Beit Shammai learn the laws of betrothal from the Hebrew maidservant.
If he paid a dinar for her, she can keep deducting down to a *perutah*. But if he paid a *perutah*, what could she deduct from? A *perutah* is the smallest sum there is.
The Gemara objects: perhaps the Torah means that a sale for a dinar allows deduction, while a sale for a *perutah* simply allows none.
The logic: a redemption that works by steady reduction assumes an original price large enough to reduce.

illustration.caption: Chizkiya's reading of *ve'hefdah* (11b): a maidservant sold for a dinar works her price down year by year, but a price of a perutah leaves nothing to deduct. The Gemara then asks whether a perutah sale might simply have no deduction.

children.continues: Continues on 12a: the objection is rejected by comparing deduction to designation, betrothal is learned from the Hebrew maidservant, the Gemara explains why the minimum is a dinar rather than two *perutot* or half a dinar, and Rava gives another reason.

key_terms.sense: the smallest legal unit of monetary value
key_terms.definition: The smallest copper coin, and the lowest value the halakha treats as money; many monetary laws apply only to something worth at least a perutah.
key_terms.on_this_daf: Beit Hillel's minimum for betrothal. The Gemara tests whether Torah "money" can be a perutah, and whether a Hebrew maidservant could be sold for one.

key_terms.sense: a woman's presumed insistence on her dignity
key_terms.definition: The presumption that a woman is particular about her own dignity and would not agree to a demeaning arrangement, such as being betrothed for a trivial sum.
key_terms.on_this_daf: R. Zeira's reason for Beit Shammai's dinar, limited after Abaye's objection to betrothal at night or through an agent.

key_terms.definition: The high-value silver coinage of Tyre, the standard for sums of money fixed by the Torah, such as the sacred shekel.
key_terms.on_this_daf: Rav Asi's rule, first stated for all Torah money and then restricted to set sums, and Rav Yosef's basis for Beit Shammai's silver dinar.

key_terms.definition: The local coinage of the Sages' time, which bore the same coin names as Tyrian coinage but was worth one-eighth as much; sums fixed by rabbinic law are reckoned in it.
key_terms.on_this_daf: Rav Asi's real addition: the Sages' fine of a sela for striking another is a provincial sela, half a dinar.

key_terms.definition: A specific amount of money fixed by law, as opposed to a requirement of "money" with no sum stated.
key_terms.on_this_daf: Rav Asi's rule is restated to apply only to set sums, so money mentioned without a sum, like betrothal money, can be any coin.

key_terms.sense: admitting part of a monetary claim
key_terms.definition: A defendant who admits part of a claim and denies the rest; by Torah law he must take an oath on the part he denies.
key_terms.on_this_daf: The oath requires a claim of only two silver ma'ah, which challenges Rav Asi's rule; the Gemara explains it from the pairing of "money" with "vessels".
aliases: admission to part of a claim

key_terms.definition: A Jewish girl sold by her father into service; she goes free at set times and may be redeemed, and her master may designate her as a wife for himself or his son.
key_terms.on_this_daf: R. Shimon ben Lakish grounds Beit Shammai's minimum in the laws of the Hebrew maidservant, from which they learn betrothal.

key_terms.sense: deduction from a servant's redemption price
key_terms.definition: The rule that a Hebrew servant who redeems himself or herself before the term ends pays the purchase price reduced in proportion to the time already served.
key_terms.on_this_daf: Chizkiya learns it from ve'hefdah, and R. Shimon ben Lakish argues that a perutah price would leave nothing to deduct.

judgment_calls: The section at 11a.6 is not headed "Mishnah:" because it returns to the chapter's opening Mishnah (Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel on the minimum) rather than opening a new one.

The discussion of Rav Asi's rule 'itself' (11a.10–11b.8) could be a separate top-level section, since it tests the rule on its own terms. It is kept under Rav Yosef's explanation because it serves to establish, and finally limit, his basis for Beit Shammai.

The four challenges to Rav Asi could be a single section with a chart. They are split into children so that each Torah case and its answer is its own step, and so that the admission-to-part-of-a-claim challenge, which the shiur does not discuss, can be flagged separately.

The restatement of Rav Asi's rule (11b.6) could be the last step of the betrothal challenge, which triggers it. It is made a sibling section because it answers the whole series and reshapes the rule used in what follows.
R. Zeira's exchange with Abaye is kept as one section rather than splitting off Abaye's objection, since the objection and answer only define the scope of R. Zeira's reason.
coverage_notes: The shiur's material on 11a.1–11a.5 (simfon, Ulla's reason, the Canaanite slave's blemishes, the thief or kuvyustus, Tosafot and Rabbeinu Chananel on kuvyustus, and the practical differences of accepting blemishes and handing her to the husband's agents), and its opening framing on Bavli vs. Yerushalmi, fall before this outline's first line and are left out.
The shiur's discussion of kiddushei bia (the Tosefta's 'le'shem kiddushin', common-law marriage, and Rav Henkin vs. Rav Moshe Feinstein) is not tied to any line in this scope and is left out.
The admission-to-part-of-a-claim challenge (11b.1–11b.2) is not discussed in the shiur; outlined from the Gemara text only.
The essay says R. Yannai's daughters would demand 'a basketful of gold coins'; the text says three kav of dinars. Followed the text.

The essay says that if she knowingly accepts 'even a perutah', even Beit Shammai concede; the text's case is R. Yannai's daughter accepting one dinar, and R. Zeira says only that knowing acceptance is outside his rule. Followed the text and did not state the perutah case.

The essay presents the challenges to Rav Asi as betrothal first, then hekdesh and ma'aser sheni, and omits the admission challenge; the text's order is admission, ma'aser sheni, hekdesh, betrothal. Followed the text.
The essay attributes the maidservant argument to R. Shimon ben Lakish without Chizkiya; the text has R. Shimon ben Lakish citing Chizkiya's reading of ve'hefdah. Followed the text.

The essay presents the maidservant argument as establishing that the price must exceed a perutah; the text at 11b.10 immediately objects that a perutah sale might simply allow no deduction, and the answer comes on 12a. Followed the text.
The essay spells the amora 'Rav Assi'; the text has Rav Asi. Followed the text.
The shiur's point that the move from 'more than a perutah' to 'a dinar' is still open refers to 12a.3, outside this scope; noted only in 'continues'.
